questions.explain: The standard topology keeps public subnets for load balancers and bastion only, with production databases in private subnets — isolated database subnets have no route to the internet at all.
options: Databases and applications both in public subnets, separated by NACLs
Databases in private subnets that still require an internet gateway route for patching
Production databases in public subnets with strict security groups; applications in private subnets
Public subnets for load balancers and bastion only; every production SQL Server in a private subnet with no public IP and no internet gateway route
questions.q: According to the chapter, what belongs in public subnets and where does every production SQL Server live?

questions.explain: On Azure SQL, explicitly set public network access to Deny and use Private Link/private endpoints; the default-allow posture is the misconfiguration.
options: Leave public network access at its default because Azure blocks threats automatically
Set public network access to Deny — the default-allow posture is the misconfiguration — and use private endpoints
Use IP firewall rules as the primary access control and keep public access enabled
Public access can stay enabled as long as TLS is enforced
questions.q: On Azure SQL, what is the correct public-access posture and why?

questions.explain: Default deny with explicit allow: 1433 reachable only from application-tier security groups, referencing security groups (not IPs) so autoscaling doesn't break the rules.
options: Allow 1433 from 0.0.0.0/0 and rely on SQL authentication for protection
Allow 1433 from the whole VPC for operational simplicity
Allow 1433 only from the application subnets' security groups — never from 0.0.0.0/0 — and reference security groups, not IP addresses
Block 1433 at the security group and allow database traffic only over the load balancer
questions.q: What is the firewall discipline for port 1433?

questions.explain: Peering is non-transitive, so transitive paths must be designed explicitly; the forgotten return route is the classic peering failure.
options: Peering is non-transitive — A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C — and route tables must be updated on both sides, including the return route
Peering requires a NAT gateway on each side for database traffic
Peering encrypts traffic automatically, so TLS enforcement can be disabled
Peering is transitive, so A automatically reaches C
questions.q: VPC peering connects A↔B and B↔C. What must the network designer remember?

questions.explain: The client must validate the server certificate (TrustServerCertificate=false in production connection strings), with TLS 1.0/1.1 disabled and certificate rotation planned.
options: TrustServerCertificate=true so clients don't fail on certificate validation
Certificate validation may be skipped on private networks since they're trusted
The client must validate the server certificate — TrustServerCertificate=false in production — with a TLS 1.2+ floor
TLS enforcement is only needed for public endpoints
questions.q: For TLS on SQL Server connections, what production setting is required?
